props.title: Slither
props.initialSlug: Alien parasites turn townspeople into zombie mutants

sections.content: **Slither** (2006) marks James Gunn's directorial debut, brilliantly fusing 1980s creature features with quick-witted comedy. The film draws clear inspiration from **The Thing** (1982) and **Night of the Creeps** (1986), featuring parasitic aliens that transform residents of a small South Carolina town into zombie-like hosts. Nathan Fillion channels his **Firefly** charm as Police Chief Bill Pardy, while Elizabeth Banks delivers a standout performance as Starla Grant, whose husband (played by Michael Rooker) becomes the primary host for the alien invasion. Gunn's signature blend of horror and humor would later influence films like **The Cabin in the Woods** (2012).

sections.content: The practical effects in **Slither** deserve special attention, deliberately echoing the grotesque body horror of **The Fly** (1986) and **Society** (1989). The film's creature designs by Todd Masters pay homage to Rob Bottin's work while establishing their own memorably disgusting identity. The meat-store sequence and Grant's transformation showcase some of the best practical effects work of the 2000s, standing alongside **The Host** (2006) and **Pan's Labyrinth** (2006) in keeping practical monster effects alive during the CGI boom.

Gunn's script cleverly subverts horror tropes while embracing genre conventions. Like **Shaun of the Dead** (2004), it functions both as parody and genuine horror. The film's small-town setting and character dynamics recall **Tremors** (1990), while its body horror elements draw from **Shivers** (1975) and **The Brood** (1979), creating a unique hybrid that influenced later horror-comedies like **Tucker & Dale vs Evil** (2010). sections.content: **Slither** represents a crucial bridge between classic creature features and modern monster movies. Its influence can be seen in films like **The Mist** (2007) and **Super 8** (2011), which similarly balance practical effects with CGI enhancements. The film's DNA carries through to Gunn's later work, including **Guardians of the Galaxy** (2014), where his ability to blend comedy with genuine emotion and spectacle reached a broader audience.
